title: Bit Manipulation Idioms — Get, Set, Clear, Toggle
summary: Get, set, clear, and toggle a single bit are the four mask-based idioms every bit-manipulation question builds on. Learn the one-line recipes, how they generalize to whole ranges, and the off-by-one and overwrite traps that catch candidates.

slides.markdown:
Four operations cover almost every bit-manipulation interview question that isn't XOR-specific: **get** a bit's value, **set** it to 1, **clear** it to 0, and **toggle** it. Each is a one-liner built from the [bitwise-fundamentals](bitwise-fundamentals) primitives plus a **mask** — an integer with 1s exactly where you want to act.

Once these four are automatic, you can build a mask for a range instead of a single bit and the same four idioms scale up unchanged. That's the whole idea behind bitmasked flags, bitsets, and — later in this group — representing entire subsets as one integer.

slides.subTitle: 1 << i is the whole trick
slides.markdown:
Every one of the four idioms starts from the same building block: `1 << i`, an integer that is 0 everywhere except a single 1 at position `i` (counting from the least-significant bit as position 0).

`1 << 0` is `0001`, `1 << 3` is `1000`. That single-bit mask is what you AND, OR, or XOR against your value to affect exactly bit `i` and nothing else — the other bits of the mask are 0, so ANDing with them forces those positions to 0, ORing with them leaves those positions untouched, and XORing with them leaves those positions untouched too.

Memorize `1 << i` as "the mask for bit i" and the rest of this topic is just picking which of AND/OR/XOR to combine it with.

slides.subTitle: AND, OR, XOR against one mask
slides.markdown:
Take `x = 0110 0101` and mask `1 << 3 = 0000 1000`. Setting is `x | mask`: every other bit stays because ORing with 0 changes nothing, and bit 3 becomes 1 regardless of what it was. Clearing is `x & ~mask`: `~mask` is `1111 0111`, all 1s except bit 3, so ANDing preserves every other bit and forces bit 3 to 0. Toggling is `x ^ mask`: bit 3 flips, every other bit XORs against 0 and is untouched.

The common thread across all three: the mask has exactly one 1, and each operator's "identity" value (0 for OR and XOR, 1 for AND) is what protects every bit outside that one position.

slides.sectionTitle: Working on a range of bits
Using OR when you meant overwrite
slides.markdown:
`x | (1 << i)` **sets** bit `i` to 1 — it can never turn a bit off. A common bug is reaching for OR when the intent was actually "make bit `i` equal to this new value, whatever it currently is," including turning it off.

`x |= (1 << i)` when the new value is `0` does nothing at all, silently, because OR-ing with 0 never clears a bit that's already 1. The correct pattern for "set bit i to an arbitrary boolean `v`" is **clear then conditionally set**: `x = (x & ~(1 << i)) | (v << i)` — clear the bit unconditionally first, then OR in the new value shifted into place. Skipping the clear step is the single most common bug in idiom code that otherwise looks correct.

Bit 0 is universally the **least-significant bit** in every idiom on this topic — `1 << 0` is the rightmost bit, not the leftmost. Candidates who've worked more with 1-indexed arrays sometimes assume "bit 1" means the first bit from the left, or that indexing starts at 1, and both assumptions break every formula here silently.

A related off-by-one: a range `[lo, hi]` inclusive spans `hi - lo + 1` bits, not `hi - lo`. Forgetting the `+ 1` when building `(1 << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1` produces a mask that's one bit too narrow, clearing or reading one fewer position than intended — a bug that often passes small test cases (where the missing bit happens to be 0 already) and fails on real data.

When in doubt, sanity-check with a concrete small example: for `lo = 2, hi = 4`, that's bits 2, 3, 4 — three bits — and `hi - lo + 1 = 3` confirms it.

Nothing about get/set/clear/toggle actually requires the mask to have exactly one 1 — that was just the simplest case to introduce them. A mask with 1s at positions `{1, 3, 4}` sets, clears, or toggles **all three of those positions simultaneously**, in the same single operation, because every bit position is handled independently and in parallel.

This is the bridge to the rest of the group: a mask *is* a subset of positions, so "set these bits" is really "add these elements to the set," and "clear these bits" is "remove these elements." `bitmask-subsets`, later in this group, builds directly on this — an entire subset of up to 20-ish items fits in one integer, and membership, union, and intersection are exactly AND, OR, and XOR on masks wider than one bit.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up outside interviews
slides.markdown:
Bit idioms aren't just an interview warm-up — they're how real systems pack data tightly. **Unix file permissions** are a single integer where bits 0-2 are "other," 3-5 are "group," 6-8 are "owner," each a read/write/execute triple you get/set/clear with exactly these idioms. **RGBA colors** pack four 8-bit channels into one 32-bit integer, and extracting the red channel is `(color >> 16) & 0xFF` — a range-read idiom.

**Feature flag registers** in large services often pack 32 or 64 boolean flags into one integer column instead of 32 separate boolean columns, because checking a flag is one AND instead of a separate memory fetch. The idioms you just learned are exactly the read/write layer for all three.

A clean answer to "how would you toggle bit 5" has three parts, and skipping any one of them reads as shakier than it should:

1. **Name the mask.** "`1 << 5` is a mask with a single 1 at position 5."
2. **Name the operator and why.** "XOR, because XOR-ing with a 1 flips that bit and XOR-ing with a 0 leaves every other bit alone."
3. **State the edge case if one exists.** "If I needed to set it to a specific value rather than flip it, I'd clear first, then OR in the new value — OR alone can't turn a bit off."

The next topic, XOR Properties and the Single-Number Family, takes XOR specifically and pushes it further: the same self-canceling property that makes toggle work is also what solves an entire family of "find the one different element" problems in O(1) space.
